summary: Defines a formal notation for specifying how fields are encoded in compressed formats when creating new ROHC profiles. It provides a library of common encoding methods to simplify future profile work. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A shared way of writing the rules for shrinking packets, so new shrinking recipes are easier to write.

subtitle: A precise, reversible way to write down how each header field is squeezed in a ROHC compression profile.

tldr.problem: Earlier header compression profiles were described with English text and ASCII boxes, which was sometimes unclear and ambiguous for complex compressed formats.
tldr.mechanism: ROHC-FN is a declarative notation where each field is tied to an encoding method with the two-way operator =:=, so one definition covers both compression and decompression. It ships a library of common encoding methods.
tldr.outcome: Profile authors get a rigorous way to define compressed and uncompressed formats and the relationship between them. It covers only the formats; the control logic of a profile must be defined by other means.

today: RFC 4997 is a Proposed Standard from July 2007, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on the ROHC framework in RFC 4995.

sections.title: Why a Formal Notation
sections.content:
ROHC-FN (Robust Header Compression - Formal Notation) helps people define ROHC header compression profiles (see RFC 4995). Earlier profiles used English text together with ASCII box drawings, which the RFC says was sometimes unclear and ambiguous when structures and encodings got complex.

The main goal is a more rigorous way to define header formats, compressed and uncompressed, and the relationships between them. The RFC says no other formal notation met these needs. It also provides a library of often-used encoding methods, so new profiles do not have to redefine them from scratch.

Scope is deliberately limited. ROHC-FN specifies the relationship between compressed and uncompressed formats. A complete profile still needs context management, feedback rules and robustness principles defined by other means.
sections.plainLanguage: People used to describe how to shrink packets using words and pictures, and different readers understood them differently. This gives everyone one exact way to write the rules down.

sections.title: Fields, Encodings and Two-Way Matching
sections.content:
A header is divided into fields. Each field has attributes: UVALUE and ULENGTH for the uncompressed form, and CVALUE and CLENGTH for the compressed form. A field is written with a dot, for example rtp_seq_number.UVALUE.

The notation field =:= encoding_method; reads as "is encoded by". It is not an assignment. It is a two-way mapping between the compressed and uncompressed attributes, resolved by two-way matching, similar to unification in logic. When compressing, the uncompressed attributes are known and the compressed ones are matched against them. When decompressing, it goes the other way. One definition therefore describes both directions.

For example, the static method succeeds at the compressor only if the context value and the uncompressed value are the same. At the decompressor it succeeds only if a valid context entry exists. A binding that fails makes the whole format unusable.

Both forms are bit strings, most significant bit first. The bit string is the value modulo 2^length, so a value of -1 in an 8-bit field is sent as 255. Inside expressions, ROHC-FN uses the full range of integers.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a secret code where one rule book tells you how to turn a message into code and also how to turn the code back. You only write the rule once, and it works both ways.

sections.title: Identifiers, Expressions and ENFORCE
sections.content:
A ROHC-FN specification is case sensitive, written in 7-bit ASCII, and consists of constant definitions, an optional global control field list and one or more encoding method definitions. The language is declarative and referentially transparent, with no side effects.

Identifiers must start with a letter, and constant names must be all upper case. Reserved words such as ENFORCE, THIS, VARIABLE, UVALUE, CVALUE, UNCOMPRESSED, COMPRESSED, CONTROL, INITIAL and DEFAULT cannot be used as identifiers. Encoding method and constant names have global scope; formats and fields are local.

Expressions look like ANSI-C with differences: no limit on integer range, x ^ y means exponentiation, and there are no assignment, bitwise or comma operators. Integers can be decimal, binary (0b prefix) or hexadecimal (0x prefix). Comments start with //.

An ENFORCE(expression); statement adds a condition that must hold for a format to be usable. If it is false, the format cannot be used. If it is true, or if it contains undefined terms, the binding is created, and undefined terms become bound. So it works both as a test and as an assignment. Lengths have a shorthand in square brackets, such as field_1 [ 4 ];, and VARIABLE marks a length defined elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like the rules of a small board game: what names you may use, how you do the sums, and a special card, ENFORCE, that says "this must be true or you cannot play this move".

sections.title: The Library of Encoding Methods
sections.content:
The library holds six commonly used methods:

  • uncompressed_value(len, val) for a field with a fixed or computable value. It sends zero bits. The IPv6 version field is uncompressed_value(4, 6).
  • compressed_value(len, val) for control fields that exist only in the compressed format, such as padding or a discriminator. A quoted bit string like '01101' is shorthand for it.
  • irregular(len) copies the uncompressed bits unchanged, so no compression happens. It is the fail-safe, for example for the TCP checksum.
  • static takes the value from the context and sends zero bits.
  • lsb(num_lsbs_param, offset_param) sends only the least significant bits of a value that differs a little from the context value.
  • crc(...) computes a CRC using the algorithm of RFC 4995.

For lsb, the interpretation interval runs from ref_value minus offset_param up to ref_value plus (2^num_lsbs_param - 1) minus offset_param. The example tcp_sequence_number =:= lsb(14, 8192) takes 14 bits and can convey values from 8192 below the context value to 8191 above it. The compressor may not know the exact reference value the decompressor holds, so it must pick parameters that stay correct for every candidate value; if it cannot, lsb fails and a less efficient format is chosen.
sections.plainLanguage: The library is a toolbox. One tool says "this never changes, skip it", one says "just send it as is", and one says "only send the last few digits because it is close to last time".

sections.title: Defining Encoding Methods and Formats
sections.content:
New encoding methods are written as a name, optional parameters in parentheses, and a body in braces. The body can contain several blocks:

  • UNCOMPRESSED lists the fields of the uncompressed header in order. Their lengths must add up to the length of the field being encoded.
  • COMPRESSED lists the fields of a compressed format in the order they are sent, which may differ from the uncompressed order. Fields that compress to zero bits can sit anywhere or be left out.
  • CONTROL declares fields that are not in the uncompressed header but have an uncompressed value, for example an IP-ID behaviour indicator that helps pick better compression.
  • INITIAL sets starting context values so that static or lsb can work on the first packet of a flow.
  • DEFAULT gives default encodings that formats use for any field they do not bind themselves.

Contiguous compressed fields can be grouped with colons and encoded as one combined bit string. The keyword THIS refers to the field being encoded, for example THIS.ULENGTH.

A method may define several compressed formats. The compressor may pick any combination whose bindings all succeed. Since the decompressor must tell the formats apart, each format should carry a discriminator, a control field that identifies it. Methods not defined in the notation, such as a profile-specific checksum inference, are referenced by name plus a quoted pointer to where they are defined.
sections.plainLanguage: You build a bigger recipe from smaller ones. You list the ingredients in the original order, then list how each one is packed for the trip, and give each packing style a label so the person unpacking knows which style was used.

sections.title: Worked Example: Compressing IPv4
sections.content:
The overview section builds a compressed format for the IPv4 header, using the method name ipv4_header. The uncompressed list gives the field widths: version 4, header_length 4, dscp 6, ecn 2, length 16, id 16, reserved 1, dont_frag 1, more_fragments 1, offset 13, ttl 8, protocol 8, checksum 16, src_addr 32 and dest_addr 32.

Five fields (header_length, version, reserved, offset and more_fragments) use uncompressed_value, so they cost no bits. The address, length, id, ttl, protocol, dscp, ecn and dont_frag fields use irregular, so they are sent unchanged. The checksum uses a profile-specific method, inferred_ip_v4_header_checksum, which recomputes it from the other fields and sends zero bits.

The RFC says this example illustrates the notation and is not the optimum way to compress IPv4 headers. Appendix B of the RFC walks through bit-level examples in more depth.
sections.plainLanguage: For an address label with many boxes, some boxes always say the same thing, so you skip them. Some change every time, so you copy them. And one is a total that the receiver can add up for itself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security section is brief. It describes ROHC-FN as a formal notation similar to ABNF and therefore not believed to raise any security issues. It notes that ABNF has a completely separate purpose from the ROHC formal notation.
sections.plainLanguage: It is only a way of writing rules down, like a spelling system, so the authors do not think it creates any new security danger by itself.

items.label: Fixed value
items.desc: Value known from an expression or constant; zero compressed bits.

items.label: Control value
items.desc: Field that exists only in the compressed format, such as padding or a discriminator.

items.label: Copy as is
items.desc: Compressed bits identical to the uncompressed field; no compression.

items.label: From context
items.desc: Same as a previous header in the flow; zero compressed bits.

items.label: Least significant bits
items.desc: Sends only low bits of a value close to the context value.

items.label: CRC
items.desc: CRC over a block of data, using the algorithm of RFC 4995.
